title: Minimal residual disease and relapse surveillance in osteosarcoma: an action-linked framework integrating liquid biopsy and imaging biomarkers

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Minimal residual disease and relapse surveillance in osteosarcoma: an action-linked framework integrating liquid biopsy and imaging biomarkers》：研究问题的原文依据。

【From molecular lead time to actionable lead time · p0095】The translational interpretation is more important than the lead-time number itself. In recurrent osteosarcoma, outcome is repeatedly linked to disease burden, metastatic distribution and resectability. Late relapse, fewer nodules, unilateral pulmonary disease and achievement of second complete remission are favorable, whereas bilateral lung disease, multiple nodules, extrapulmonary metastases, local recurrence accompanying metastasis and progression during treatment identify patients less likely to undergo complete surgical clearance [6], [7], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. Surveillance innovation should therefore aim to detect recurrence before the transition from solitary or oligometastatic disease to multifocal, less resectable dissemination. Molecular lead time becomes actionable lead time only if it triggers earlier anatomical confirmation, MDT review, metastasectomy assessment, local therapy planning, trial referral or a safe reduction in unnecessary surveillance burden.

【Risk inputs and dynamic updating · p0180】A practical surveillance workflow can combine three input layers, each supported by a different type of evidence. The first is established clinicopathological risk: metastatic disease at diagnosis, axial or proximal tumor site, large tumor volume, elevated alkaline phosphatase or lactate dehydrogenase, surgical margin status and poor histological response to preoperative chemotherapy [2], [3]. The second is molecular risk: postoperative ctDNA or cfDNA methylation positivity, persistent positivity after adjuvant chemotherapy, dynamic conversion from negative to positive, or rising quantitative burden [25], [36]. The third is imaging-derived risk: suspicious chest CT or local MRI findings, poor functional MRI response such as limited ADC increase or low rWIR, and candidate high-risk radiomics signatures [51], [54], [59], [60]. The purpose is not to replace clinical judgment with a score, but to update risk as new evidence appears during treatment and follow-up.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Minimal residual disease and relapse surveillance in osteosarcoma: an action-linked framework integrating liquid biopsy and imaging biomarkers》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Designing prospective biomarker-guided surveillance studies · p0245】Future studies must move beyond asking whether biomarkers predict relapse and ask whether biomarker-guided surveillance improves management. The supporting evidence should be translated into study-design requirements rather than treated as a clinical guideline. The most informative first step for osteosarcoma would be a prospective, multicenter, longitudinal cohort embedded within routine follow-up. Patients should be enrolled at diagnosis or at the completion of curative-intent therapy, tumor tissue should be collected for tumor-informed MRD when planned, and serial blood sampling should be synchronized with standardized chest CT and local MRI intervals. Molecular conversion, imaging changes and clinical relapse should then be mapped on the same timeline so that each biomarker signal can be evaluated as a decision trigger rather than as an isolated prognostic observation. External solid-tumor experience supports this logic but should not be overgeneralized: ctDNA studies in localized lung cancer showed that molecular relapse may precede radiological progression, whereas the randomized DYNAMIC trial in stage II colon cancer demonstrated that ctDNA-guided management can be tested as an interventional strategy with predefined actions and clinical endpoints [76], [77]. Osteosarcoma needs the same type of action-linked evidence, not simple transfer of thresholds from other tumors.

【Endpoints beyond earlier detection: Resectability, second remission, trial access and patient burden · p0250】Predefined endpoints should distinguish earlier detection from improved care. They should include radiological relapse, event-free survival, overall survival, time from biomarker positivity to imaging relapse, proportion of biomarker-positive episodes that become anatomically localizable, resectability at recurrence, metastasectomy rate, achievement of second complete remission, local therapy planning, treatment modification, trial enrollment, false-positive investigations, radiation and visit burden, patient anxiety and quality of life. For ctDNA, protocols should prespecify positivity thresholds, panel failure rules, minimum plasma input, turnaround time and management of molecular-positive/imaging-negative results [19], [20], [25]. For methylation, CTCs, extracellular vesicles and miRNAs, assay normalization and cut-offs must be reproducible before clinical interpretation. For imaging biomarkers, thresholds such as rWIR <2.3 or radiomics risk scores require prospective testing against predefined relapse and survival endpoints rather than retrospective optimization [54], [59], [60]. Diagnostic-accuracy reporting standards such as the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) provide a useful reminder that sensitivity, specificity, timing, reference standards and indeterminate results should be reported transparently before a surveillance test is treated as decision-grade evidence [74].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Minimal residual disease and relapse surveillance in osteosarcoma: an action-linked framework integrating liquid biopsy and imaging biomarkers》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusions · p0275】Conventional imaging-based follow-up remains essential in osteosarcoma because relapse must be anatomically confirmed before curative salvage can be attempted. However, imaging alone does not fully capture the earlier biological phases of recurrence in which residual viable cells, micrometastatic disease and molecular relapse may precede radiological visibility. This review argues that the next step is not a single replacement biomarker, but an action-linked surveillance model that connects molecular timing, anatomical localization, imaging-derived phenotype, discordant-result management and predefined clinical action. Tumor-informed ctDNA currently provides the strongest molecular MRD evidence, while cfDNA methylation, CTCs, extracellular vesicles and circulating miRNAs remain complementary but less mature signals. Functional MRI and radiomics contribute local viability and candidate risk-stratification information, but most imaging biomarker evidence still derives from response, prognosis or retrospective modeling rather than validated surveillance intervention. Clinical translation will require harmonized assays, reproducible imaging protocols, explicit action and non-action thresholds, prespecified discordant-result pathways, multicenter longitudinal validation and endpoints that show improved resectability, trial access, patient-centered burden or survival. Integrated biomarker-guided surveillance may become a clinically useful bone oncology workflow only if molecular or imaging lead time can be converted into actionable benefit rather than earlier documentation of relapse alone.

【Chest CT, chest radiography and the problem of actionable detection · p0080】The unresolved issue is not whether imaging is needed, but how intensive, how long and how adaptive it should be. Osteosarcoma-specific follow-up series support early, lung-focused surveillance but do not establish a universally optimal imaging modality or interval [29], [30]. The practical interpretation of the CT-versus-radiography literature is not that one modality should replace all others, but that earlier radiological detection is valuable only when it preserves a salvage option. Paioli et al. reported that CT-based follow-up was associated with higher second complete remission rates and better post-relapse outcomes than chest radiography in selected patients with lung-only recurrence, whereas Rothermundt et al. argued from a smaller extremity osteosarcoma cohort that chest radiography could detect lung relapse when metastasectomy remained possible and that routine CT should be balanced against radiation exposure [29], [30]. The updated randomized TOSS study across limb sarcomas similarly found no survival disadvantage with less intensive surveillance despite earlier pulmonary metastasis detection by CT [31]. Thus, current evidence supports imaging as the anatomical backbone while also showing why surveillance innovation must be judged by actionable outcomes, not by earlier detection alone.

sections.title: 复现线索
sections.text:
《Minimal residual disease and relapse surveillance in osteosarcoma: an action-linked framework integrating liquid biopsy and imaging biomarkers》：复现时可直接核对的数据、软件或实现线索。

【MDT implementation, patient communication and equity · p0260】MRD-guided surveillance should not simply add blood tests to fixed imaging schedules; it should personalize follow-up intensity only when personalization is shown to be safe and useful. Persistently negative MRD, low-risk imaging features and favorable clinicopathological factors could be tested as criteria for surveillance de-escalation, including lower imaging frequency, reduced radiation exposure, fewer hospital visits, less sedation burden and lower scan-related anxiety. Conversely, persistent or rising ctDNA, high-risk cfDNA methylation, suspicious CTC dynamics, adverse radiomics signatures or poor functional MRI response could justify earlier imaging and MDT review within a predefined research protocol [25], [26], [54]. Patient burden must be measured rather than assumed. A systematic review of surveillance imaging after treatment for childhood extracranial solid tumors found insufficient evidence that routine imaging improves survival in most diseases and highlighted radiation exposure, scan volume, cost-effectiveness uncertainty and the lack of psychological distress data as major gaps [78]. A broader systematic review of postoperative cancer surveillance reported that scanxiety is common, often concentrated around the scan-to-results interval, and not reliably reduced by simply modifying surveillance schedules [79]. These data support inclusion of patient-reported anxiety, waiting time, false-positive investigations, cumulative imaging exposure and family burden as endpoints in osteosarcoma surveillance studies.

【MDT implementation, patient communication and equity · p0265】Implementation also determines whether promising evidence can become a bone oncology workflow. Tumor-informed assays require tumor tissue availability, sequencing capacity, bioinformatics support and turnaround times compatible with clinical milestones. However, real-world implementation is constrained by assay feasibility. In the Fu et al. study, customized MRD panels could not be generated in 12 of 83 patients, indicating that tumor-informed monitoring may not be universally applicable because of insufficient sequencing targets, technical limitations or other assay-related factors [25]. For patients without an available tumor-informed assay, standard imaging-based surveillance remains essential, and alternative molecular approaches should currently be considered investigational rather than assumed replacements for ctDNA monitoring. In pediatric and adolescent populations, longitudinal liquid biopsy strategies also require consideration of patient-specific factors, including blood volume limitations, venous access, sampling frequency and cumulative burden associated with repeated blood collection [26].
